tagline: Cross mountain passes and orchard valleys before returning by island and ferry.
intro: The Cascade Loop links Puget Sound, mountain passes, orchards, eastern Washington’s shrub-steppe and Whidbey Island in a 440-mile circuit. Designated a National Scenic Byway in 2021, it is promoted by State of Washington Tourism for mountain landscapes, farmland and island views. The tourism office lists nine hours of driving and recommends five days for the trip. The circuit includes three other scenic byways: Stevens Pass Greenway, North Cascades Scenic Highway and Whidbey Scenic Isle Way. The Cascade Loop Association divides the journey into nine regions with distinct landscapes.

The roads that make the circuit possible arrived decades apart. The Stevens Pass Highway opened in 1925, providing Washington’s second automobile crossing of the Cascades. The North Cascades Highway’s final 30 miles opened in September 1972, after construction began in 1961. Anticipating new tourist traffic, Winthrop’s businesses backed a downtown remodeling project in 1971, adding Old West false fronts and wooden boardwalks.

From Everett, follow US 2 toward Stevens Pass, then descend through Leavenworth to the Wenatchee Valley’s orchards. Continue by Chelan and Pateros into the Methow Valley before crossing Washington Pass on Highway 20. The westward return runs through the Skagit Valley, crosses Deception Pass to Whidbey Island, and heads south to the Clinton–Mukilteo ferry.

moments.title: Leavenworth
moments.text: Leavenworth’s Bavarian town center began as a deliberate response to economic decline. The Great Northern Railway relocated to Wenatchee in 1925; mills closed, shops moved and Leavenworth’s population continued falling into the 1950s. Project LIFE formed in 1962 to investigate revival, and businessmen Ted Price and Bob Rodgers promoted an alpine theme. In 1965, Price and Rodgers led a trip to Solvang, California, whose Danish-themed buildings offered an example for the proposed transformation. The fire-damaged Chikamin Hotel became the first Bavarian-style conversion, reopening as the Edelweiss in July 1965. By 1970, a design review board was enforcing the new architectural standards.

moments.title: Washington Pass
moments.text: The Washington Pass overlook faces Liberty Bell Mountain and a stretch of highway 700 feet below. A 0.2-mile trail connects the pass to that viewpoint; it became a National Recreation Trail in 1978. Washington Pass reaches 5,477 feet on State Route 20. Rainy Pass lies about four miles west, and the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the highway there. Delancy Ridge is also visible from Washington Pass; the North Cascades Highway follows the southern base of that four-mile-long ridge. These high crossings close seasonally because of snow; the complete loop depends on the North Cascades Highway’s reopening.
moments.notice: Liberty Bell Mountain rises beyond the overlook, with Highway 20 visible 700 feet below.

moments.title: Deception Pass
moments.text: Before a bridge joined Fidalgo and Whidbey islands, travelers summoned the unscheduled ferry by striking a saw with a mallet. Construction began in August 1934, and the bridge was dedicated on July 31, 1935. The Public Works Administration and county funds financed the $482,000 construction, replacing the earlier ferry connection. The crossing actually uses two bridges, with Pass Island between Canoe Pass to the north and Deception Pass to the south. The northern crossing has a steel arch; the southern span uses cantilever construction. During ebb and flood tides, swift currents can form standing waves and whirlpools visible from the pedestrian walkways.

practical: Washington Pass: Highway 20 closes annually for snow and avalanche risk. WSDOT typically closes mileposts 134–171 from late November until late April or early May. (checked 2026-10-11)
